item.title: Gold price falls nearly 3% as CPI tops forecasts, lifting dollar and yields

item.dc:creator: Mining.com
item.content:encoded: Gold prices fell nearly 3% on Tuesday after hotter-than-expected US inflation data lifted the dollar and Treasury yields while reinforcing expectations of a bigger interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve this year. Spot gold XAU= was down 2.8% at $4,021.36 per ounce by 11:33 a.m. ET (1635 GMT). US gold futures GCcv1 for December delivery fell 1.9% to $4,036.00 per ounce. “I think it’s a bit of a short-term negative for gold because the inflation numbers were running a little higher than expected,” said Edward Meir, an analyst at Marex. The US Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% last month after advancing 0.6% in September, the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast a 0.3% month-on-month rise. Bets on a 50-basis-point Fed rate hike in December started to build after the inflation print and comments by Fed governor Christopher Waller, who said he would support more aggressive action in the event of a too-hot Consumer Price Index report. The probability of a 25 bp hike is fully priced in, while the possibility of a 50 bp hike rose to 10.5% from 0% before the data, according to CME’s FedWatch Tool. The US dollar .DXY rose against a basket of other major currencies, and Treasury yields climbed. A stronger dollar makes gold more expensive for overseas buyers, while higher Treasury yields increase the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion. “(Gold) continues to trade above the critical $4,000/oz mark,” Standard Chartered said in a note, adding “crude oil, inflation risks and equity markets continue to set the tone of trading for gold with a focus on rate hike expectations for the December Fed meeting.” Meanwhile, the Monetary Authority of Singapore said it would launch a vaulting service to hold bullion for foreign central banks and lower taxes on some companies in the gold market as it competes for a bigger slice of the precious metals trade. Spot silver XAG= fell 3.9% to $51.32 per ounce and palladium XPD= was down 2.0% at $1,021.22. (Reporting by Vedika Thorat and Anjana Anil in Bengaluru; Editing by Kirsten Donovan and Jonathan Ananda)

item.title: US CPI Exceeds Expectations Again, Waller's Warning Comes True! Wall Street Focuses on Whether December Rate Hike Will Be 25 or 50 Basis Points; "New Fed News Agency": Stop-and-Go Strategy Faces Test
item.description: The "New Federal Reserve Newsletter" pointed out that before the release of the CPI, Waller suggested the possibility of a 50-basis-point rate hike in December, and so far, no other Fed officials have publicly responded. In addition to a single 50-basis-point hike, the Fed may also choose to signal consecutive rate hikes in December and January. Wall Street generally believes that inflationary pressures remain stubborn, further strengthening the case for a rate hike in December, though a 50-basis-point increase is not a consensus. The market is concerned about whether the Fed will extend the tightening cycle.
item.dc:creator: 华尔街见闻
item.content:encoded: US inflation in October once again exceeded expectations, further raising market expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike in December, with the possibility of a larger rate increase now being discussed. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) announced on Tuesday, November 10, that the October CPI rose 0.4% month-on-month, lower than the 0.6% increase in September but higher than economists’ forecasts of 0.3%. The core CPI rose 0.3% month-on-month, matching September’s increase and exceeding the market’s expectation of 0.2%. This marks the third consecutive month where overall CPI rose more than Wall Street predicted, and core CPI has also climbed 0.3% month-on-month for three straight months. Due to the failure to collect CPI data during the US federal government shutdown in October 2025, the BLS was unable to provide a year-on-year figure for October CPI. This report precisely meets the policy threshold previously outlined by Federal Reserve Governor Waller. Just hours before the CPI was published, Waller stated that if the core CPI for October increased by 0.3% or more month-on-month, he might support a 50 basis point rate hike at the Fed’s monetary policy meeting in December. With this criterion now met, the market’s bets on a 50 basis point rate hike in December have gained momentum. Nick Timiraos, a journalist nicknamed the “New Fed Whisperer,” pointed out that this inflation report is testing the Fed’s previous strategy of “spacing out rate hikes,” using staggered moves to leave room to monitor economic data. The choices facing policymakers are not only between a 25 or 50 basis point hike in December, but also whether to adjust the pace of subsequent actions, or even to signal back-to-back rate hikes in December and January of next year. Wall Street’s reaction is showing a common assessment: inflationary pressures remain stubborn, providing more justification for a December rate hike, though opinions differ on the size of the increase. Some believe that three consecutive months of core CPI climbing 0.3% makes it difficult for the Fed to ignore the inflation rebound; others feel that a 50-basis-point hike may be too aggressive and that 25 basis points is still the more realistic option. The market’s real concern is not just the decision at the next meeting but also whether the Fed may extend the tightening cycle as a result. “New Fed Whisperer”: Core prices strengthen across the board, Fed could signal back-to-back hikes In his analysis in The Wall Street Journal, Timiraos noted that the strong showing of October inflation is testing the Fed’s strategy of spreading out rate hikes across different meetings to allow time to observe economic data. He noted that Waller has raised the possibility that if the third month’s inflation data remains hot, a 50-basis-point rate hike in December could be on the table. However, no other Fed officials have publicly echoed this position as of yet. The Fed could also choose another way to address inflationary pressures: instead of a one-off 50-basis-point increase at a single meeting, it could signal consecutive rate hikes in December and January. According to Timiraos, this could be one way to adjust the policy pace. The last time the Fed raised rates by more than 25 basis points at once was back in 2022. On social media, Timiraos further broke down the details of core inflation, pointing out that core prices “strengthened broadly” in October. Specifically, core goods prices rose at a 1% annualized pace over the past six months, compared with just 0.1% in the previous period through June; core services prices excluding shelter rose 0.4% in October, about 4.9% annualized, while three- and six-month annualized increases stood at 5.5% and 3.2% respectively. He also pointed out that the unrounded month-on-month increase in core CPI for October was 0.296%, marking the third straight month at about 0.3%. The three-month annualized rate for core CPI climbed to 3.75%, compared with only 1.6% in July. This data shows that inflationary pressures are not just driven by overall energy price increases—core goods and services prices are also consistently strengthening. For the Fed, this makes it harder to treat inflation as a short-term shock and simply wait for price pressures to subside on their own. Waller raises 50-basis-point option, market begins to reassess policy strength Just hours before the CPI was released, Waller gave a hawkish speech while attending an event in London. He said the US economy was experiencing strong growth and a stable labor market, but inflation remained too high, requiring the Fed to “tighten policy sooner rather than later.” Waller had previously supported the Fed’s decision to keep rates unchanged at the last meeting, arguing that previous policy communications had already led financial markets to price in some degree of tightening. He believes policy adjustments do not have to be implemented in consecutive meetings, but prior guidance on rate hikes must eventually be delivered on, otherwise markets may lower expectations for further tightening, causing financial conditions to ease prematurely. Regarding the December meeting, Waller had already indicated before the CPI was published that if the October core CPI once again rose by around 0.3% month-on-month (as in the previous two months) or even higher, more forceful policy action might be needed. He explicitly raised the possibility of a 50-basis-point hike, and warned that if inflation remained high and price pressures broadened, raising rates by only 25 basis points could hurt the Fed’s credibility in fighting inflation. Ultimately, the October core CPI met this threshold. According to Reuters, after the data was announced, market expectations for a 25-basis-point rate hike in December were almost certain, and bets on a 50-basis-point hike rose to about 15% at one point. The two-year US Treasury yield surged, recording its largest single-day rise since early April 2025. However, Timiraos also cautioned that no other Fed official has publicly echoed Waller’s 50-basis-point position so far. Thus, the market’s discussion of a larger rate hike does not necessarily mean consensus within the Fed. Wall Street divided: Inflation pressures cannot be ignored, but 50 basis points is not a consensus After the inflation data was released, several Wall Street figures said the reasons for a December Fed rate hike had increased, but assessments of the scale and the persistence of inflation pressures varied. Omair Sharif, President of Inflation Insights, commented that the latest report “offers little to ease market concerns about persistent inflation risks” and does not dispel the Fed’s reasons for further hikes. He also estimated that the October core PCE price index might climb by 0.34%, representing an annualized increase of over 4%, higher than the previous month. While the Fed’s 2% policy target is based on headline PCE inflation, core PCE better reflects the underlying inflation trend. If this estimate is confirmed by subsequent data, it would further justify Fed tightening. James McCann, Senior Economist at Edward Jones, described this as another “disappointing inflation report,” reflecting that underlying price pressures may be building again. With US economic growth and the labor market both clearly accelerating this year, and core inflation showing signs of reacceleration, the Fed faces even greater policy pressure. McCann pointed out that the real worry is whether inflation is settling at a higher level. He argued the report at least solidifies the rationale for a 25-basis-point hike in December, while the bigger debate has become whether the Fed needs a 50-basis-point hike and more aggressive action. Peter Cardillo, Chief Market Economist at Spartan Capital Securities, also believes a December rate hike is virtually certain, with the suspense lying in whether it will be 25 or 50 basis points. He commented that Waller has effectively paved the way for a half-point hike, and the latest data shows inflation remains an issue. However, Cardillo also cautioned that circumstances could still change over the next 30 to 40 days. Should oil prices retreat and pass through to consumer prices, inflationary pressures may ease; but if oil rebounds, the inflation outlook could deteriorate again. Chris Zaccarelli, Chief Investment Officer at Northlight Asset Management, believes inflation above an ideal level further increases the likelihood of a December Fed hike. Still, despite market calls for a 50-basis-point hike, he expects the Fed will only lift rates by 25 basis points next month. Joe Saluzzi, Co-Head of Themis Trading, likewise noted that persistently high core inflation shows that price pressures have “stickiness” and that a 25-basis-point hike remains realistic, while 50 basis points may be too aggressive. He also warned that prolonged high rates and inflation will continue to pressure borrowing-dependent businesses, affecting profits and stock valuations. Skyler Weinand, Chief Investment Officer at Regan Capital, stated that the latest CPI paves the way for another Fed rate hike in December—the central bank cannot ignore the clear rebound in inflation data. He also pointed out that the latest jobs report showed robust employment gains in October as well as upward revisions to previous months’ data, providing the Fed with more room for further hikes. Labor market remains resilient, tightening policies may persist longer Besides inflation itself, the continued resilience of the US labor market also provides the Fed more leeway to prioritize combating inflation in its policy decisions. In his speech on Tuesday, Waller noted that US unemployment fell to 4.1% in October, with 165,000 new jobs added that month and a combined upward revision of 85,000 jobs over the prior two months. Although the average monthly jobs gains over the past six and twelve months is about 80,000, the overall labor market remains in a broadly balanced state, with no significant deterioration. This means the Fed, faced with persistently high inflation, need not worry about the impact of rate hikes on jobs as much as it would if the labor market were visibly weakening. Brian Jacobsen, Chief Economic Strategist at Annex Wealth Management, pointed out from a price transmission angle that three consecutive months of core CPI rising 0.3% month-on-month shows that the issue isn’t just high headline CPI, but that energy shocks may have begun to seep into core inflation. He also mentioned that Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee previously discussed how AI demand could be a new source of inflationary pressure for the Fed. As AI investment and infrastructure expansion rise, economic activity may crowd out resources in other areas and push up prices for some services. Jacobsen suggests the Fed may increasingly focus on the resource squeeze from AI demand and rising wage costs for skilled trades like plumbers and electricians. Jeff Schulze, Chief Investment Strategist at Franklin Templeton Institute, warned that the latest inflation data will serve as a headwind for risk assets. Investors are beginning to price in a 50-basis-point December hike and more afterward; rising short-term yields and a stronger US dollar could both suppress equity valuations. Karen Manna, Fixed Income Investment Strategist at Federated Hermes, also said the report strengthens the rationale for another Fed rate hike and further demands policymakers maintain vigilance. The real concern for investors is that if inflation remains high, the Fed may have to keep monetary policy restrictive for an extended period, well into 2027. Overall, the October CPI brings a December rate hike closer to market consensus, but the policy options facing the Fed are no longer just whether to raise rates. Waller’s 50-basis-point option, Timiraos’ comments on rate-hike spacing, and whether other officials will support speeding up the pace of tightening—all will be key market focuses going forward.

item.title: CPI Deals a Blow to US Bonds! 2-Year Yield Surges Over 20 Basis Points Intraday, Gold and Silver Plunge
item.description: After the release of the CPI, traders began to expect a lower likelihood of a 50 basis point rate hike in December; this year’s Federal Reserve voting member Logan stated that a faster pace of rate hikes may be needed this winter, with at least two more 25 basis point hikes required before pausing. Subsequently, the rise in U.S. Treasury yields continued to widen, with the 10-year yield climbing back above 5.0% and rising more than 10 basis points intraday; spot gold once fell over 3%, while spot silver at one point dropped more than 4%.
item.dc:creator: 华尔街见闻
item.content:encoded: In October, U.S. inflation once again exceeded market expectations, triggering a sell-off in U.S. Treasury bonds and a sharp rise in yields across the board. The strengthening U.S. dollar and heightened expectations for higher interest rates also put pressure on gold and silver. With Federal Reserve officials repeatedly sending hawkish signals, markets are not only increasingly betting on a rate hike in December but are also beginning to assess the possibility of a larger hike and further monetary policy tightening into next year. On Tuesday, U.S. Eastern Time, after the release of the U.S. CPI data, U.S. Treasuries were heavily sold, sending prices plunging and yields accelerating higher. The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield expanded its gains following the CPI release and, after remarks by Federal Reserve official Lorie Logan, briefly broke above 5.01% during the U.S. stock market midday session, rising more than 10 basis points on the day. The 2-year Treasury yield, which is more sensitive to Fed policy expectations, climbed even more, surpassing 4.77% during midday and jumping more than 20 basis points on the day, on course for its biggest single-day surge since April last year. Precious metals markets also came under pressure. After the U.S. CPI release, gold extended its losses during the session. In the U.S. stock market midday, New York gold futures hit an intraday low of $4,020.8 per ounce, dropping nearly 2.3% on the day; spot gold fell below $4,014 per ounce, down nearly 3.1% intraday. The decline in silver was even more pronounced. Market data shows that at the day's lows in New York's midday, silver futures fell nearly 3% intraday, while spot silver plunged over 4%. CPI Inflation Continues to Beat Expectations for Months, Bond Market Reprices Fed Policy Path The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Tuesday that October CPI rose 0.4% month-on-month, higher than the market expectation of 0.3%, but slowed from 0.6% in September. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy prices, also rose 0.3% month-on-month, surpassing expectations of 0.2% and matching September’s increase. This marks the third consecutive month of 0.3% gains for core CPI. Due to the U.S. federal government shutdown at the same time last year, which prevented data collection, the Bureau did not release year-on-year CPI data for October. Just hours before the CPI data was released, the market was already rattled by hawkish remarks from Fed Governor Christopher Waller. In a speech in London on Tuesday, Waller said that even if inflation improved in October, he would still be inclined to support a 25 basis point Fed rate hike in December. However, if core CPI reached 0.3% or higher for a third straight month, the Fed should consider a 50 basis point hike in December. He warned that raising rates by only 25 basis points could undermine the credibility of the Fed’s fight against inflation. The actual core CPI published hit Waller’s 0.3% threshold precisely. After the data release, markets quickly ramped up bets on a larger rate hike. Reuters reported that traders’ implied probability of a 50 basis point hike by the Fed in December spiked to about 13.6%, from near zero before the data was released; by contrast, a 25 basis point hike had already become the mainstream market expectation. According to Bloomberg, the inflation data triggered a sell-off in Treasuries, with short-term maturities bearing the brunt. Money markets also increased bets that the Fed will hike rates at least two more times by mid-2027, and began more clearly pricing in the possibility of a one-off 50 basis point hike in December. Lindsay Rosner, Head of Multi-Sector Fixed Income Investing at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, said that if CPI remains robust, the Fed may usher in a more aggressive tightening cycle. Her view reflects market worries over persistently high inflation: even if a December hike is now the baseline expectation, future policy rates could still be more hawkish than previously anticipated. This Year’s FOMC Voter Logan: Faster Rate Hikes May Be Needed This Winter, Fed Needs at Least Two More 25 Basis Point Hikes Before a Pause Following the CPI release, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan also sent further signals of policy tightening. Logan is a voting member of the FOMC this year. Speaking at an energy conference co-hosted by the Dallas Fed and the Kansas City Fed on Tuesday, she said that given current economic and inflation prospects, the Fed still needs to implement at least two additional 25 basis point hikes. Logan noted that the specific pace of hikes depends on the near-term economic and financial environment, and that the Fed might need to move faster this winter than it has this autumn. She stated, "It may be necessary this winter to act more quickly than the FOMC has so far this autumn." However, Logan is not advocating for continuous rate hikes. She said that after completing these two hikes, the Fed could pause to assess the economy and financial markets before deciding on further policy adjustments. She also emphasized that if inflation remains above target for an extended period, it could gradually become entrenched in business and household expectations, making timely action crucial. Logan’s comments signal that some Fed officials are discussing not just whether to hike rates in December, but also how to reach a moderately restrictive level more quickly. Her statements echoed Waller’s, further fueling market concerns about the Fed tightening policy even more over the coming months. U.S. Treasury Yields and Dollar Rise Together, Doubling Pressure on Gold and Silver Both U.S. Treasury yields and the dollar are strengthening, putting pressure on non-yielding precious metals. On one hand, higher bond yields increase the opportunity cost of holding non-interest-bearing assets like gold and silver; on the other hand, a stronger dollar makes dollar-denominated precious metals more expensive for holders of other currencies. According to Reuters, after October inflation data came in higher than expected, gold prices fell noticeably as the market began evaluating the chances of the Fed taking a more aggressive rate-hiking stance. Gold is especially sensitive to changes in interest rate expectations, and if the market further raises its outlook for policy rates, precious metals could continue to face pressure in the short term. However, the future path for gold and silver will not depend solely on Fed policy. Movements in the dollar, geopolitical risks, energy prices, and investors’ outlook on the economy can all affect demand for precious metals. The key market shift currently is that both the inflation data and hawkish comments from Fed officials have reinforced expectations for higher rates, forcing a reset in precious metals trades that previously benefited from rate-cut expectations.
